extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, programme managers, and science policy analysts interested in peer review and bibliometrics
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and evaluate the design features, goals, and quality metrics of peer review used to assess manuscripts, grant applications, research groups and institutions, and how bibliometric indicators are linked to peer review. Focus is on the criteria and dimensions that determine peer review quality and operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymity / Blinding (single-blind vs double-blind)
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees can remain anonymous or be named; the researchers under review can be anonymous or their names can be visible to the referees (‘double-blind’ vs. ‘single-blind’).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a design choice affecting potential bias and fairness; the article frames it as one of several structural variables that can be set differently across contexts (no prescriptive judgment but highlights as a key variant).

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of Referees and Mode of Interaction
rubrics_metrics.description: An evaluation can be carried out by one referee or by several. If a group of referees is used, the members can evaluate the work independently or work with the others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choices affect reliability and consensus: multiple independent referees may reduce idiosyncratic judgments, while group discussion can lead to negotiated outcomes; the review notes variation across applications and contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permanency of Referees (permanent vs ad hoc)
rubrics_metrics.description: A referee can be deployed on a permanent or an ad hoc basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permanent panels bring institutional memory and standardisation; ad hoc reviewers bring specific expertise and flexibility. The trade-offs influence consistency, expertise fit, and potential biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality vs Public Review
rubrics_metrics.description: The peer review process can be designed to be accessible to the public or it can be confidential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public processes increase transparency and accountability; confidential review may encourage frank assessments. The article discusses this as a key structural dimension but does not prescribe a single best option.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of Formalization / Specification of Evaluation Criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: The evaluation can be undertaken in accordance with highly formalised specifications, but the selection of criteria on which to judge the work can also be left to the referees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formalised criteria promote comparability and reproducibility of judgements; leaving criteria to referees allows contextualised expert judgement. The review highlights this as a tension affecting standardisation and validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referee Expertise as a Primary Quality Criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Proponents consider active scientists to be the most suitable people to evaluate the scientific quality of work done by colleagues in their own field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expertise enables appropriate methodological and conceptual judgements; the article presents this as a core rationale for peer review’s legitimacy (experts can assess standards, logic, and methodological appropriateness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tasks of Referees: Selection, Error Detection, and Improvement Suggestions
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees are tasked with recommending the ‘best’ scientific research given scarce resources and possibly formulating suggestions for improvement; they are also supposed to find errors in scientific work or incorrect scientific conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peer review is framed both as a gatekeeping/filter function ('filter to separate the wheat from the chaff') and as a mechanism to improve submissions through constructive feedback and integrity checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goal: Quality Control and Merit-based Assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review should be a filter to separate the wheat from the chaff, and thus to guarantee and improve the quality of published research; when it works, merit rather than influence determines what is published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This expresses the normative objective of peer review—ensuring experiments/data meet standards, results follow logically, and publication is meritocratic rather than influence-driven.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliability of Decisions (consistency across referees)
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics: Different referees do not agree on the assessment of the same scientific work (lack of reliability).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reliability is a central evaluative metric for peer review procedures; variation in judgements across reviewers is cited as a key weakness and a target for empirical study and procedural design (e.g., number of reviewers, standardisation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness / Bias (systematic, non-scientific influences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics: Recommendations from referees are systematically biased. The work is judged not only on its scientific quality, but also on non-scientific criteria (lack of fairness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fairness includes avoidance of nepotism, network effects, and bias against certain groups or ideas; design choices like blinding, bibliometric checks, and transparent procedures are discussed as ways to manage bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity of Judgements (correspondence to true quality/outcomes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics: The correlation between the judgements in the peer review process and the quality of the refereed work is low (lack of validity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Validity is raised as a problem when peer judgements do not predict downstream success or true scientific quality; the review notes limited empirical consensus and calls for more rigorous study of peer review effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Bibliometrics to Inform Peer Review (‘Informed Peer Review’)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nowadays it is recommended for major evaluation contexts to use an informed peer review process where the peers are informed by bibliometric indicators. Bibliometric analysis will never be a substitute for peer review, but, if the analysis is comprehensive and sound, it should inform peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bibliometrics can strengthen transparency and substantiate decisions; they are presented as complementary tools that can inform and verify referee judgements, not replace expert judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bibliometrics as Verification and a Check on Network Effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicators have an important function in that they subject the evaluations from a peer review to verification and thus protect them from the ‘old boys’ network effect’.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using standardized indicators can provide an external check on subjective decisions, helping to detect nepotism or systematic biases; however, indicators require careful standardisation and interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for Expert Interpretation and Contextualisation of Bibliometric Indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct evaluation of scientific performance in accordance with formalised and context-independent criteria and without additional interpretation is impossible; bibliometric indicators would require annotation by an expert and enhancement and correction from an awareness of the context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantitative indicators must be read by domain experts who can specify relevance, account for disciplinary norms, and assess implications for individuals and institutions; this supports combined peer/bibliometric approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining Peer Review and Bibliometrics for Balanced Evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of both methods, with the peer-reviewer having access to bibliometric indicators, permits the reviewer to form an evaluation that emerges from comparison between his/her personal subjective judgment and the quantitative indicators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article endorses a complementary model: juxtapose subjective expert judgement with standardised metrics to balance pros and cons of each, acknowledging context and objectives will determine relative weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection Challenge: Positive Selection vs Negative Selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Whereas in the past referees’ task was negative selection (filtering out work below a minimum standard), today they have to choose the best from many, frequently very good, research applications (positive selection).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive selection increases difficulty and risk of type-I/II errors in funding/publication decisions; it has consequences for applicants (rejection of worthy projects) and funders (lower likelihood that funded projects will later be unsuccessful).
